[THOUGHT]  
The case presents a 7-year-old male with insidious left knee pain and antalgic gait, no trauma or systemic symptoms. Physical exam of the knee is entirely normal, raising suspicion for referred pain — a classic presentation of Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (LCPD), where hip pathology (especially early avascular necrosis of the femoral head) manifests as knee or thigh pain. Radiographs show *flattening and fragmentation of the left femoral head* on bilateral hip views — findings that are pathognomonic for the fragmentation stage of LCPD. These changes are not seen in transient synovitis, SCFE, septic arthritis, JIA, or malignancy, all of which have been explicitly excluded by imaging and clinical features. The age (peak incidence 4–8 years), sex (male predominance ~4:1), unilateral involvement, and absence of red flags (fever, lab abnormalities, effusion, physeal disruption) further reinforce LCPD as the diagnosis. Radiographic confirmation is definitive; no additional testing is required to establish the diagnosis.
